title: Sealing joist ends and ceiling junctions for airtightness
subtitle: Closing the air path where floor joists meet the external wall at ceiling level
excerpt: The junction between the top of a masonry wall and the ends of floor joists is one of the largest unintentional air-leakage paths in an older house. Cold air flows through the cavity or past the mortar around joist ends and emerges into the floor void or up behind the ceiling finish.
sourceNotes: STBA guidance on airtightness in traditional buildings; BRE Trust report BR 262 section 6 on floor-to-wall junctions; Energy Saving Trust CE290 guidance on draughtproofing.

glossaryTerms.definition: The section of a floor or ceiling joist that sits on the wall plate or is built into the masonry at the wall, where the joist transfers its load to the wall.
A route through a building element that allows uncontrolled air movement between inside and outside, increasing heat loss and reducing comfort.

content.text: Where a floor joist is built into a masonry wall, the mortar around the
cracks and shrinks over decades. That crack opens a direct

from the cavity or the external wall into the floor void and from there into the room. In a cold snap you may feel a draught running along the skirting board or from behind the coving at ceiling level; that is this junction leaking.

On a cold windy day, run the back of your hand along the skirting board and the coving on external walls. A draught cool enough to feel indicates air movement from behind the ceiling or floor void. An incense stick or a dampened paper held near the same line shows airflow more clearly in milder conditions.

Without opening the ceiling or floor, access to the joist end is limited. The most effective sealing from inside is to fill the gap between the skirting board, the floor, and the wall with a continuous bead of silicone or acrylic caulk, and to tape the coving-to-wall and coving-to-ceiling junctions with a flexible sealant. This does not seal the joist end itself but closes the path from the void into the room.
Remove the skirting board carefully (a bolster chisel and patience). The gap behind the skirting between the floor and the wall face is where cold air enters the room.
Fill the gap along the base of the wall behind the skirting with low-expansion foam. Allow to cure before trimming flush.
Refix the skirting board; seal the skirting-to-floor and skirting-to-wall junctions with a paintable acrylic caulk. Smooth with a damp finger.
For the ceiling junction: apply a bead of acrylic caulk behind the coving and at the coving-to-wall joint. Where coving is absent, apply sealant directly at the ceiling-to-wall junction.
The thorough approach: from inside the floor void

Where access to the floor void is possible (suspended timber ground floor via a crawl space, or a first floor via a loft hatch), apply low-expansion foam around each joist where it meets the wall plate. Pay particular attention to the gap between the joist end, the wall plate, and the external masonry.

rows.symptom: Draught still present at skirting level after sealing
rows.cause: Air path enters through the floor surface as well as behind the skirting, floorboard gaps near the wall
rows.fix: Fill the first two or three floorboard gaps near the external wall with a flexible sealant or papier-mâché fill.

rows.symptom: Sealant at skirting-to-wall joint cracks within one winter
rows.cause: Rigid silicone or plaster filler was used; thermal movement opens the joint
rows.fix: Replace with a flexible acrylic caulk rated for building movement joints (look for Class 12.5 on the label).
